title: Motion to Intervene and Comments of ITC Great Plains, LLC in support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s 02/10/2026 filing proposing revisions to the Open Access Transmission Tariff under ER26-1323.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                 )
    Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                   )                   Docket No. ER26-1323-000
                                                 )


                           MOTION TO INTERVENE AND
                  SUPPORTING COMMENTS OF ITC GREAT PLAINS, LLC

           Pursuant to Rules 213 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 ITC Great Plains, LLC (“ITC Great Plains”)

moves to intervene and submits these comments in support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s

(“SPP”) February 10, 2026 filing proposing revisions to the SPP Open Access Transmission

Tariff (“Tariff”) to add Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (“CHILLS”) that will allow

High Impact Large Loads (“HILLs”) to be served with non-firm, conditional transmission

service.

      I.      MOTION TO INTERVENE

           ITC Great Plains is an independent, stand-alone transmission company engaged

exclusively in the development, ownership, and operation of facilities for the transmission of

electric energy in interstate commerce. ITC Great Plains is a subsidiary of ITC Holdings Corp.

ITC Holdings Corp. invests exclusively in the electric power transmission grid to improve

electric reliability, facilitate access to low-cost generation resources, improve access to power

markets, and reduce the overall cost of delivered electric power. Transmission service over

facilities developed and owned by ITC Great Plains is provided by SPP pursuant to its Tariff.

ITC Great Plains is a Transmission Owner member of SPP.


1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.213, .214 (2025).
             As an SPP Transmission Owner, ITC Great Plains would be subject to the CHILLS

requirements proposed herein. Thus, ITC Great Plains has a specific, direct, and substantial

interest in the outcome of this proceeding. ITC Great Plains has unique interests that cannot be

adequately represented by any other party. Accordingly, ITC Great Plains requests the

Commission grant this Motion for Leave to Intervene in this proceeding and permit it to become

a full party for all purposes.

      II.      COMMENTS

            As demonstrated in SPP’s filing, the proposed CHILLS is a just and reasonable, critical

component of SPP’s innovative effort to rapidly and reliably integrate exponentially increasing

large loads in the SPP region. As the Commission found in its order accepting SPP’s HILL and

High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA,” together, “HILL/HILLGA”)

processes, “unprecedented growth in large loads in the SPP region presents significant and

unique operational and planning challenges.”2 And although the HILL/HILLGA processes are

foundational to SPP’s response to these challenges, these processes do not themselves enable

transmission customers limited by existing resources and/or required network upgrades to

expeditiously acquire transmission service for HILLs. The proposed CHILLS bridges this gap

and, by utilizing the information produced by the HILL/HILLGA processes and pursuant to

stakeholder-honed requirements designed to preserve reliability, allows transmission customers

to procure non-firm, conditional transmission service for HILLs for up to seven years. As

highlighted below, several aspects of SPP’s proposal should be viewed as best practices for other

regions that are similarly confronting the challenges posed by integrating and serving large loads.




2
    Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031, at P 60 (2026).

                                                  -2-
 The CHILLS proposal compliments and effectuates SPP’s just and reasonable HILL/HILLGA

processes, and ITC Great Plains respectfully urges the Commission to also accept the CHILLS

proposal as just and reasonable.

                 a. SPP’s Proposal Properly Requires that CHILLs Be Studied and Metered on
                    a Gross Basis
          SPP’s proposal appropriately requires that HILLs receiving CHILLS (i.e., “CHILLs”)3 be

studied and metered on a gross basis rather than netted against any supporting generation to

avoid cost-shifting and adverse effects to reliability. SPP cogently identifies the problems

inherent in netting the withdrawals of large loads such as HILLs against their supporting

generation:

                    Because these loads are so large, they may pose significant
                    operational challenges for SPP’s operation of the Transmission
                    System. For example, if a HILL is supported by Behind-The-Meter
                    Generation, the net load on the Transmission System may be quite
                    small relative to the true size of the load. […] If the supporting
                    generation trips, and the full load is served by the Transmission
                    System, it may create transmission congestion or require Operating
                    Reserve deployment.4

          In short, netting the withdrawals of CHILLs against their supporting generation would

obscure CHILLs’ actual use of the grid and the benefits they derive therefrom, introduce the

possibility for large instantaneous load changes on the system, and increase transmission prices.

To avoid these effects and reliably serve CHILLs, SPP proposes to study each CHILL to

determine its CHILLS Reserved Capacity, which is the “maximum amount of capacity and




3
 SPP proposes to define Conditional High Impact Large Load as “[t]he portion of a High Impact
Large Load that is eligible to connect to the Transmission System and receive CHILLS.” SPP
Transmittal at 1 n.2.
4
    Id. at 32.

                                                  -3-
 Energy that the Transmission Provider agrees to transmit for the Transmission Customer,”5 and

to charge CHILLs for transmission service and Schedule 11 Base Plan Zonal Charges and

Region-wide Charges based on this value without netting it against the output of the CHILL’s

supporting generation.6 Further, SPP’s proposal requires each CHILL, firm load, and generation

located at the same point of delivery to submit separate real-time telemetry and bill meter values

“to give SPP transparent data for each CHILL in Real-Time and to correctly bill the

Transmission Customer for the load and transmission service.”7

          SPP’s proposal also ensures that transmission service taken by network load located at

the same point of delivery as CHILL and behind-the-meter generation is not improperly netted

against any excess output of that generation. If in this configuration, the CHILL amount and

output from the co-located generation exceed the CHILLS Reserved Capacity, such that the

generation is displacing the network load, that excess must be added to the network load to

ensure accurate loads (i.e., not artificially lowered by netting) are reported and billed for

Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”).8

          The non-firm, conditional service provided by CHILLS is a reasonable means of

expeditiously integrating HILLs pending the completion of required network upgrades.

However, once those network upgrades are completed, it is critical that, like the network load in

the configuration just described, HILLs procure firm service, and NITS in particular. As SPP

explained in its comments on the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued in Docket


5
    Id. at 15 n.65, 23.
6
    See Proposed Tariff, Schedule 11 §§ I, V.A.-B.; id., Schedule 15 §§ 1, 6.
7
    SPP Transmittal at 32.
8
    Id. at 26.

                                                 -4-
 No. RM26-4-000, SPP designs and constructs its system to serve load on a firm, “continuous[,]

and reliable basis.”9 No less than other loads, HILLs will receive the full panoply of benefits

provided by SPP’s system.10 Permitting HILLs to procure service other than NITS charged on a

gross basis would shift the costs caused by HILLs’ significant impact on the system to other

loads and fail to ensure affordability as large loads proliferate. Accordingly, while CHILLS is a

reasonable near-term option for HILLs, it is imperative that these loads transition to NITS so that

the rate and reliability benefits provided by SPP’s system can be realized.

                  b. SPP’s Proposal Establishes Clear Parameters, Roles, and Responsibilities
                     Concerning Curtailment
          SPP’s proposal establishes curtailment requirements for CHILLS and clearly defines the

roles and responsibilities associated therewith, preventing CHILLS from negatively impacting

the reliability of the SPP system. The proposed Tariff clearly indicates that CHILLS is subject to

curtailment on a non-discriminatory basis in the event the transmission system is constrained or

under emergency conditions or other unforeseen conditions.11 The proposed Tariff also clearly

identifies SPP as being responsible for curtailing CHILLS when such conditions threaten to

impair or degrade the reliability of the SPP system or other connected systems.12 Upon notice

from SPP of such a threat to reliability, SPP, the transmission customer, and the transmission

10
   See Otter Tail Power Co., Opinion No. 93, 12 FERC ¶ 61,169, at 61,420 (1980) (“[A]n
integrated system is designed to achieve maximum efficiency and reliability at a minimum
cost on a systemwide basis. Implicit in this theory is the assumption that all customers . . .
receive the benefits that are inherent in such an integrated system.”).
11
  SPP Transmittal at 14 (“Through the execution of a CHILLSA, Transmission Customers
accept CHILLS with full realization that such service is subject to availability . . . .”).
12
     Id. at 28.

                                                  -5-
 owner must implement load shedding and curtailment procedures agreed upon in the CHILLS

Operating Agreement prior to the commencement of service.13 Finally, should it fail to comply

with these procedures—as evidenced by the required telemetry described above—the

transmission customer is subject to penalties, just as if the transmission customer exceeds its

CHILLS Reserved Capacity during normal conditions. These requirements leave no room for

ambiguity as to each party’s responsibilities in the event curtailment is required to maintain the

reliability of the SPP system.

                  c. SPP’s Proposal Ensures the Reliability and Resilience of the SPP
                     Transmission System
           In addition to the requirements described above concerning the prohibition on netting

CHILLS withdrawals and curtailment, SPP’s proposal features comprehensive requirements

designed to ensure the continued reliability and resilience of the SPP system. Foundationally,

SPP’s proposal requires that transmission customers have supporting in-service generation

sufficient to serve the entire CHILL prior to receiving CHILLS.14 Additionally, SPP is

authorized to offer prospective CHILLS customers less than their requested CHILLS Reserved

Capacity when SPP determines that current conditions on its or any third-party systems will not

permit that requested amount,15 and although a CHILLS customer may once yearly request an

adjustment to its CHILLS Reserved Capacity, the CHILLS Reserved Capacity cannot exceed the

CHILLS Reserved Capacity originally studied and granted by SPP.16 Finally, Critical Loads—

 i.e., load critical to delivering fuel to generators or identified as critical by a regulatory

authority—are not eligible for CHILLS because “[c]urtailing these loads could exacerbate

reliability issues during extreme weather conditions.”17 These are but a few additional examples

highlighting SPP’s commitment to ensuring that CHILLs will not be able to withdraw more

energy than SPP has determined the grid will reliably tolerate.

      III.        CONCLUSION

             Building on its innovative HILL/HILLGA processes, SPP’s CHILLS proposal provides

HILLs an accelerated path to transmission service without sacrificing the reliability of the grid.

As the Commission considers similar proposals in other regions, SPP’s proposals prohibiting the

netting of service taken by CHILLs, establishing clear requirements concerning curtailment, and

mitigating various risks to reliability represent considered judgments worthy of being recognized

as best practices. For these reasons, the Commission should accept SPP’s filing as just and

reasonable.

                                        Respectfully submitted,
